title: Circles and the Apollonius locus

board_content.text: Circles, and the k=1 vs k!=1 split

board_content.caption: A circle, and a perpendicular-bisector line

board_content.text: $k=1$: perpendicular bisector (a LINE), not a circle.
Proof idea: expand with $|w|^{2}=w\bar w$; the $z\bar z$ term survives only when $k\neq1$.

segments_english.text: Circles are the other fundamental locus, and the Apollonius condition is where a subtle trap hides.
The cleanest circle is modulus of z minus z zero equals r: all points at fixed distance r from the centre z zero. That reads straight off as a circle.
The picture shows both loci: a circle of radius r about its centre, and, for contrast, a perpendicular-bisector line.
In general form, a circle is z z bar plus a bar z plus a z bar plus b equals zero, with a complex and b real, having centre minus a and radius root of the modulus of a squared minus b.
Now the Apollonius locus: the set where the ratio of distances, modulus of z minus z one over modulus of z minus z two, equals a constant k.
Here's the trap. When k equals one, the two distances are equal, so this is the perpendicular bisector, a straight line, not a circle.
But when k is positive and not equal to one, the locus really is a circle, the Apollonius circle.
The proof idea: square the condition and expand using modulus w squared equals w times w bar. The z z bar term survives only when k is not one; at k equal one it cancels, leaving a line.

segments_hinglish.text: Circles doosra fundamental locus hain, aur Apollonius condition wahan hai jahan ek subtle trap chhupa hai.
Sabse clean circle hai modulus of z minus z zero barabar r: saare points jo centre z zero se fixed distance r par hain. Ye seedha circle padha jaata hai.
Picture dono loci dikhati hai: apne centre ke around radius r ka circle, aur contrast ke liye, ek perpendicular-bisector line.
General form mein, circle hai z z bar plus a bar z plus a z bar plus b barabar zero, a complex aur b real ke saath, jiska centre hai minus a aur radius hai modulus of a squared minus b ka root.
Ab Apollonius locus: wo set jahan distances ka ratio, modulus of z minus z one over modulus of z minus z two, ek constant k ke barabar ho.
Ye raha trap. Jab k barabar one ho, dono distances equal hain, to ye perpendicular bisector hai, ek straight line, circle nahi.
Par jab k positive aur one ke barabar na ho, locus sach mein ek circle hai, Apollonius circle.

Proof idea: condition ko square karo aur modulus w squared barabar w times w bar se expand karo. z z bar term sirf tab survive karta hai jab k one na ho; k barabar one par wo cancel ho jaata hai, ek line chhodte hue.
